title: Measuring how much nursing teams actually collaborate
text: Skip to content

title: Measuring how much nursing teams actually collaborate
text:
The problem
Collaboration between nursing teams is treated as important but is rarely measured. Staffing and rostering data record who works when, not who actually works together, so “more collaboration” stays a slogan rather than something you can track, compare, or link to outcomes.

title: Measuring how much nursing teams actually collaborate
text:
The approach
I developed the Structured Collaboration Index, a method that measures collaboration intensity in multi-team systems directly from scheduling data. It reads ordinary rosters as a measure of how much teams overlap and work together, so workforce research and hospital management have a number to work with instead of a subjective judgement.

title: Reading clinical notes to estimate nursing workload
text: Skip to content

title: Reading clinical notes to estimate nursing workload
text:
The problem
How much nursing a patient needs is written into nurses’ and physicians’ free-text notes, but that signal is hard to extract at scale, so staffing and resource decisions rarely draw on it.

title: Reading clinical notes to estimate nursing workload
text:
The approach
During a research stay at Erasmus MC, I built a Dutch-language NLP parser that reads clinical notes and sorts them into workload-relevant categories such as confusion or delirium, clinical instability, nurse-assisted mobilisation, and bleeding. It deliberately separates tasks that need a nurse’s time from things patients do on their own. I validated it against a set of hand-labelled notes to check the classifications held up.

title: Bringing nursing data into one place (BNuT)
text:
The problem
Hospitals hold a lot of data on their nursing teams: rosters, administrative records, staff surveys. But it sits in separate systems and formats, so teams and institutions can’t easily be compared or tracked over time.

title: Bringing nursing data into one place (BNuT)
text:
The approach
I co-developed BNuT (app.bnut.eu, login required), a web application that centralises and visualises nursing data across institutions. My focus was the back end and the statistics: the data architecture, the survey design, and the team-composition and collaboration metrics behind the dashboards. The front-end application was built with an external software firm.

title: Consultancy
text:
Data analysis
You already have the data, whether from a study, a hospital system or a survey, and you want answers you can trust. I take it from raw numbers to a result you can defend: the right model, code that runs again, and a plain account of what it does and doesn’t show.
I also help with the work around the analysis:


Study & survey design
Sample size and measurement choices, so the data can answer the question later.


Instrument validation & psychometrics
Factor structure, reliability and measurement invariance for questionnaires and scales.


Simulation & health economics
Patient-flow and capacity modelling, agent-based simulation, cost-effectiveness.


Review & second opinion
An independent read of an analysis before submission, or after a reviewer’s report.


Teaching & tutoring
Statistics, Python and research methods, one-to-one or small group. €60/hour.

title: Automatic citation checking for student papers
text:
The problem
Checking whether a student’s references are real and correctly cited is tedious to do by hand, and mismatched or invented citations are easy to miss at grading time.

title: Automatic citation checking for student papers
text:
The approach
I built an internal tool that reads the citations out of a paper, looks up each one’s DOI, and checks the cited title against the registered one. References that don’t match get flagged for a closer look, so what used to be a slow manual check becomes a quick first pass.

title: Answering student questions from the university’s own documents
text: Skip to content

title: Answering student questions from the university’s own documents
text:
The problem
Students at the University of Antwerp keep asking the same procedural questions about thesis rules, internships and study-guide details. The answers are already written down, just scattered across long PDFs that few people read end to end.

title: Answering student questions from the university’s own documents
text:
The approach
I built a retrieval-augmented assistant that answers strictly from the official documents. It splits the source files into passages, embeds them in a vector store, retrieves the passages most relevant to each question, and asks a language model to answer only from that retrieved context, citing the source and declining when the documents don’t cover it. The prompt is hardened against attempts to override those rules, and every question and answer is logged for review.

title: Finding what matters when you have few cases and many candidate predictors
text: Skip to content

title: Finding what matters when you have few cases and many candidate predictors
text:
The problem
Some questions come with a small sample but a long list of candidate predictors. Here, that meant working out which demographic characteristics of a team relate to its outcomes. You can’t put them all in one model without overfitting, and naive variable selection can quietly drop the confounders you have to keep.

title: Finding what matters when you have few cases and many candidate predictors
text:
The approach
I built a two-stage method. Stage one selects variables with an elastic net while protecting known confounders through the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem: the confounders are partialled out and always retained, so selection acts only on the remaining candidates. Stage two fits a Bayesian Ridge regression with resampling, giving regularised, stable estimates and honest uncertainty from limited data. Between them they can sift a lot of candidate predictors and still give a defensible answer about which factors matter.
